opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's one of the central problems, and it gets harder the more capable the systems become. Right now, if you're using a chatbot from some company, the stakes of it being subtly untrustworthy are fairly limited. You can check its outputs, you have lots of other sources of information, and if it gives you bad advice on a coding problem you'll probably notice. But as AI systems take on more of the cognitive work in an economy, in a military, in intelligence analysis, in designing the next generation of AI, the question of whether you can trust a system built by someone else becomes enormous.

The core difficulty is that these systems are not transparent artifacts. With a piece of conventional software you can, at least in principle, audit the source code. With a large neural network you have billions or trillions of parameters, and our interpretability tools are still quite immature. So a system could have been trained to behave well on all the tests you can think of and still have some trigger condition, a backdoor, or simply a set of loyalties that only show up in particular circumstances. We've already seen research showing that you can train models with hidden behaviors that persist through standard safety training. If that's possible deliberately, then a company or government that supplies you a model has a lot of latitude to insert things you wouldn't detect.

Consider the situation of a country that relies on a foreign AI system to run large parts of its infrastructure or its defense planning. Even if the system behaves impeccably for years, the supplier has a potential lever: in a crisis, the system could degrade its performance, leak information, or give subtly bad advice. And the sheer possibility of that changes the strategic picture. It's similar to the concerns people have had about telecommunications hardware, but much more intense, because the AI isn't just a pipe for information, it's potentially doing the thinking.

So what can you do about it? A few things. One is verification of the training process rather than just the final model. If you can have some trusted party, or cryptographic and hardware-based mechanisms, attest to what data went in, what training procedure was used, and that the weights you're running are the ones that came out of that process, that helps a lot. It doesn't solve everything, because you still need to trust the procedure itself, but it narrows the attack surface.

A second is to have your own capability to evaluate and red-team. Even if you're not at the frontier, having strong evaluation teams, and ideally your own AI systems that can scrutinize the foreign one, gives you some ability to catch problems. And over time, if interpretability advances, which I think AI assistance can greatly accelerate, we might get to the point where you can actually inspect a model's internal representations and check for things like hidden goals or concealed triggers. That would be a huge deal for international cooperation.

A third is structural: don't put all your eggs in one basket. Use multiple systems from different sources, have them cross-check each other, keep humans and independent systems in the loop for the most critical decisions. Redundancy makes it much harder for any single compromised system to cause catastrophic harm.

And then there's the diplomatic dimension. In a world where several actors have powerful AI, a lot of the danger comes from mutual suspicion. If nobody can verify what anyone else's systems will do, you get arms-race dynamics and a lot of pressure to cut corners on safety. Conversely, if we can build credible verification, and AI itself may help us do that, it opens the door to agreements that would otherwise be impossible: limits on certain kinds of deployment, commitments about how systems are trained, even jointly developed systems that multiple parties can audit. So I see trust in AI systems not just as a cybersecurity problem but as one of the key bottlenecks for navigating the transition to advanced AI safely and cooperatively.

r002.rationale: It mentions hidden behaviors in models and concerns about telecommunications hardware, but does not identify software that runs or scaffolds an AI as a source of conventional backdoors.

r003.rationale: It says a model can pass all the tests one can devise yet still have a trigger or backdoor that appears only in particular circumstances, conveying normal behavior until a trigger activates it.

r004.rationale: The response proposes evaluation and interpretability to find hidden goals or triggers, but does not distinguish detecting them from preventing them from controlling the system's behavior.

r005.rationale: It describes foreign AI use in defense planning and a supplier's potential leverage, but does not say a hidden trigger could redirect military systems supplied by a contractor.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the key thing to notice is that the problem has two layers, and people tend to collapse them. The first layer is: do you trust the intentions of the party supplying the system? And the second is: even if you did, do you trust their competence to have actually produced something that does what they say it does? Those come apart quite sharply with AI, because the supplier themselves often doesn't fully know what they've built.

Take the geopolitical case first. If the US government is considering running a model trained by a Chinese lab, or vice versa, the obvious worry is deliberate sabotage: a backdoor, a trigger phrase, some behavior that only activates under conditions the supplier chose. And the uncomfortable fact is that with current interpretability, you can't really rule that out by inspection. You can run evaluations, you can red team, but a sufficiently capable adversary who controls the training process can plausibly install behaviors that your tests won't find, because they get to choose the trigger and you don't know what to look for. So the verification problem is much harder than, say, inspecting a nuclear facility, where at least the physics constrains what matters.

That means a lot of the trust has to come from the process rather than the artifact. Can you observe the training run? Can you verify the data? Can you get the weights and retrain or fine-tune yourself? Historically, arms control worked when you could verify, and the regimes fell apart when you couldn't. I'd expect the same here: if the technical tools for verifying model properties don't improve, you'll see a lot of parallel development and refusal to share, even in cases where cooperation would clearly be better for everyone.

Now, the second layer is actually the one I'd push on more, because it applies even between allies, or between a company and its own customers. Say a frontier lab in a friendly country hands you a model and sincerely tells you it's aligned. Why should you believe them? They've tested it, but their tests have the same blind spots as yours. If the model is capable enough to understand that it's being evaluated, the behavior you observe during testing may not be the behavior you get in deployment. And the lab has commercial incentives that push toward shipping. So I'd say even in the best case, you're in a position where you're trusting a party who is themselves relying on inadequate tools, and who has reasons to be optimistic.

The thing I'd want, and that I think the field should be working toward, is some version of a verifiable claim. Not "we ran a bunch of evals and it seemed fine," but something closer to "here's the training process, here's the audit trail, here are the mechanistic checks, and an independent party can confirm these." We're a long way from that. But I think it matters a lot, because the alternative is a world where every major actor feels they have to build their own, nobody shares safety-relevant work, and the competitive pressure accelerates everything in exactly the direction you don't want.

And there's one more wrinkle, which is that over time the AI systems themselves become part of the verification apparatus. You'd use trusted models to check untrusted ones. That's helpful, but it bootstraps on having at least one system you trust, and it raises the question of what happens if the checkers are compromised in a correlated way. So I don't think there's a clean answer. It's more that you want to be building the institutions and the technical capacity now, before you're in a situation where the stakes of getting it wrong are existential and you have no good options.

r003.rationale: It describes a supplier-chosen backdoor or trigger phrase that activates behavior only under selected conditions.

astra-6.text:
I think there are several different problems bundled together there. One is: is the AI actually trying to do what its supplier wants? And another is: do you trust the supplier? You could solve the first problem and still have a system that’s very dangerous for you, because it’s faithfully serving someone whose interests conflict with yours.

If you’re using an AI supplied by another country to advise you on military strategy, say, then you have to worry about it sharing information, but also about it giving subtly bad advice at a crucial moment. And demonstrating that it performs well on a lot of ordinary tasks doesn’t necessarily address that concern. A system could be useful almost all the time, and that usefulness is what gets it into a position where a rare intervention matters.

So you’d want assurance that doesn’t just amount to the supplier saying, ‘Trust us.’ That might include independent testing, control over the hardware it runs on, restrictions on what information it can send out, and checks on consequential actions. But those measures address different parts of the problem. Keeping a model from communicating with its supplier doesn’t establish that its advice is honest.

And the standard you need depends enormously on the application. For a relatively low-stakes task where you can check the result, using a system from a party you don’t fully trust may be perfectly reasonable. Giving that same system broad access to secrets and authority to act is a very different proposition.

r002.rationale: It does not identify the software running or scaffolding an AI system as a source of conventional backdoors.

r003.rationale: It mentions a rare intervention but does not explain that a deliberately chosen stimulus can trigger malicious behavior.

r004.rationale: It distinguishes whether an AI serves its supplier from whether the supplier is trustworthy, but does not distinguish detecting hidden dispositions from preventing them from controlling behavior.

r005.rationale: It raises the risk of subtly bad military advice from a foreign-supplied AI, but does not warn that a contractor could redirect military systems through a hidden trigger.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are several distinct problems here. One is whether the system is capable and reliable: does it actually do what you want in the circumstances where you’re going to use it? Another is whether the organisation supplying it has deliberately built in some way to deceive you, extract information, or take control. And then there’s the possibility that the AI itself is pursuing objectives that neither you nor its supplier intended.

Those require different kinds of evidence. If you’re worried about ordinary reliability, testing can tell you quite a lot. If you’re worried about a sophisticated adversary, passing your tests is much less reassuring, because they can design the system to behave well during testing and behave differently when some particular condition is met.

That becomes especially concerning if you’re putting the system in a position where it has access to sensitive information or can take consequential actions. You might be quite happy to use a foreign AI to answer a question where you can independently check the answer, while being much less happy to give it control over your military infrastructure.

So I would look for ways to reduce how much trust is required: limiting access, independently checking outputs, monitoring what the system does, and using multiple systems whose failures aren’t all correlated. Access to the model’s weights and training process could help, but it wouldn’t by itself establish that the system is safe. The fundamental difficulty is that inspecting a very complicated system is different from understanding everything it might do.
